detail.title: Sustainable valorization of lithium mine tailings into lightweight foamed ceramics driven by synergistic pore-forming mechanisms
detail.abstract: The rapid expansion of the lithium-ion battery industry has generated massive quantities of lithium mine tailings (LMT), creating severe environmental and land-occupation challenges. This study presents a novel and sustainable approach for converting LMT into high-performance lightweight foamed ceramics by synergistically incorporating blast furnace slag, diatomite, pyrite tailings, and calcined kaolin. Batch compositions were rationally designed based on the CaO-MgO-Al2O3-SiO2 phase diagram, while sintering parameters (temperature, holding time, and heating rate) were systematically optimized. Comprehensive characterization using XRD, SEM-EDS, Micro-CT, mercury intrusion porosimetry, and mechanical testing revealed that at 1150 °C with 90 min holding time and 5 °C·min-1 heating rate, the optimal formulation achieved a minimum apparent density of 0.75 g/cm3 while maintaining acceptable compressive strength. A uniform honeycomb-like pore structure with thick, continuous walls was formed through the ideal dynamic balance between liquid-phase viscosity and internal gas pressure, with gas generation primarily from SO3 decomposition and residual carbon combustion, and structural reinforcement provided by stable mullite crystals. Elemental mapping confirmed that moderate LMT addition optimized the Si/Al/Ca ratio in the glass phase, enabling superior pore uniformity and mechanical integrity. This work not only establishes an efficient, low-carbon pathway for the high-value valorization of hazardous lithium mine tailings but also offers valuable theoretical insights into pore-forming mechanisms, paving the way for sustainable lightweight insulation materials and advancing circular economy development in the lithium battery industry.

title: Leveraged Looping in Real-World Asset Markets: A U.S. Regulatory Perspective

detail.title: Leveraged Looping in Real-World Asset Markets: A U.S. Regulatory Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper examines the emerging practice of leveraged looping in markets for tokenized realworld assets (RWAs) through the lens of the rapidly evolving United States regulatory framework, with particular attention to concurrent stress in private credit markets. Leveraged looping is a yield-amplification strategy in which investors use tokenized RWAs as collateral to borrow funds on decentralized lending platforms, reinvest the proceeds in additional RWA tokens, and repeat the cycle recursively. The paper analyzes the core mechanism of recursive collateralization and identifies a fundamental structural tension between DeFi's instant settlement expectations and RWA's traditional settlement timelines. This "timing mismatch" creates novel systemic risks that are now being tested by real-world credit market conditions. The paper examines the current U.S. regulatory landscape as of March 2026, including: (1) the SEC's January 28, 2026, staff statement on tokenized securities establishing three taxonomic categories; (2) the OCC's February 25, 2026, proposed rulemaking implementing the GENIUS Act's stablecoin framework; (3) the Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC's March 5, 2026, joint guidance confirming technology-neutral capital treatment of tokenized securities; and (4) the stalled Digital Asset Market Clarity Act negotiations. The paper incorporates the March 2026 warning from Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan regarding an impending shakeout in private credit markets amid rising defaults and redemption pressures, analyzing how this turbulence affects RWA looping strategies that rely on private credit as underlying collateral. The paper argues that leveraged looping sits at the intersection of multiple regulatory regimes and market risks, and that the current private credit stress tests the fundamental assumption that RWA yields will remain stable and predictable. Three scenarios for the future of RWA looping in the United States are outlined, and the paper concludes with observations on the critical importance of the current legislative window.

title: Sources of Inequality at Birth: The Interplay Between Genes and Parental Socioeconomic Status
affiliations: University of Bologna - Department of Economics, , VU University Amsterdam, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE), Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE), University of Zurich, affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Bristol, Northwestern University and USC Center for Economic and Social Research

detail.title: Sources of Inequality at Birth: The Interplay Between Genes and Parental Socioeconomic Status

keywords: Gene-by-Environment Interplay; Genoeconomics; Polygenic indices; Social Science Genetics; ESSGN

publicationDetails.journalName: USC Center for Economic & Social Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The start of a human’s life can be characterized by two lotteries: that of your genes
(nature) and the family you were born into (nurture). These set in motion a trajectory,
from birth onward, in health and human capital. Leveraging three longitudinal socialscience
data sets, we systematically analyze the relationship between an individual’s
genotype, the socioeconomic status (SES) of the families they grew up in, and their
realized traits in adulthood. We proxy an individual’s genetic predisposition by polygenic
indexes (PGIs) and family SES by a latent factor of parental education and father’s
(former) occupational status. We then investigate how PGIs, parental SES, and their
interaction contribute to later-life outcomes across a range of forty-five socioeconomic,
anthropometric, health, behavioral, and personality traits. We find strong genetic
and socioeconomic associations

title: Deep-Level History: A Complex Systems Methodology for Quantifying the Trajectory of Humankind   [Series Paper #3: The Super-Invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind]

detail.title: Deep-Level History: A Complex Systems Methodology for Quantifying the Trajectory of Humankind   [Series Paper #3: The Super-Invention Taxonomy and Direction of Humankind]

declarations.ethicsApproval: This research had no patients/participants.
declarations.funderStatement: There was no funding for this research.

detail.abstract: This paper establishes the historiographical and methodological foundation for a multiyear quantitative research sequence. It initiates a paradigm shift by replacing the subjective "search for meaning" in history with the mathematical determination of "direction." The author argues that traditional historical analysis fails because it focuses on the "history of events"-a chaotic surface layer equivalent to ocean waves. In its place, this paper introduces deep-level history, a subsurface current of humankind's development analogous to the Gulf Stream. By applying complex systems theory to humankind as a single emergent entity, the methodology demonstrates how to filter historical noise to reveal a consistent, measurable trajectory. To validate this approach, a quantitative proof of concept is provided using the development of the United States between 1780 and 1820. This framework provides the necessary theoretical justification for the super-Invention taxonomy and the subsequent high-resolution modeling of humankind's development across a multi-million-year timeline.

title: Converting EBITDA Multiples into Hurdle Rates

detail.title: Converting EBITDA Multiples into Hurdle Rates
detail.abstract:
Setting a market-derived EBITDA multiple equal to the discounted cash flow expression for the same enterprise value and canceling EBITDA from both sides yields a simple bridge equation: M = f ÷ (WACC − g), where M is the EBITDA multiple, f is the ratio of free cash flow to EBITDA, g is the long-run growth rate, and WACC is the required rate of return. The equation converts in either direction: a known market multiple implies a specific hurdle rate, and a known hurdle rate implies the multiple that income and market approaches must agree on. 

The bridge equation reframes the market approach as a hurdle rate discovery exercise rather than a comparability exercise. Every arm's-length EBITDA transaction embeds a required return; the bridge equation extracts it. When that embedded rate is applied in the income approach, the two methods reconcile by construction. When the income approach uses a rate inconsistent with any documented buyer class, the bridge equation identifies the source of the disconnect — not the math, but the input. 

The article derives the equation, illustrates its application in both directions, develops a practitioner framework for its use, and examines what it reveals about standard CAPM build-up methodology when applied to closely held business valuation.

title: A Hedonic Pricing Model for Graded Pokémon Trading Cards

detail.title: A Hedonic Pricing Model for Graded Pokémon Trading Cards
detail.abstract: We apply hedonic pricing methodology to the secondary market for graded Pokémon trading cards, focusing on Special Illustration Rare and Illustration Rare cards from fourteen Scarlet & Violet expansion sets released between 2023 and 2026. Using transaction-level data on 360 cards with verifiable PSA-graded sales activity, we estimate log-linear hedonic regressions in which the dependent variable is the natural logarithm of average eBay PSA 10 sale prices, and explanatory variables include raw market price, rarity status, set fixed effects, character popularity tiers, an interaction term capturing differential elasticities across rarity classes, an empirically identified top-tier artist indicator, a hype-divergence proxy derived from price-tracker market signals, and a within-set sales-velocity z-score. The fully specified model achieves an R² of 0.879 (adjusted R² of 0.870). Raw card price exhibits a robust elasticity of approximately 0.48, with significantly steeper price transmission for Special Illustration Rares than for Illustration Rares. Top character tiers, top artist identification, and the hype-divergence proxy all contribute statistically and economically significant explanatory power. An appendix documents an experimental extension using CLIP image embeddings, which yields only marginal improvement in fit and motivates a discussion of the limits of computer-vision features in this market segment. Themethodology described in this paper underlies the H6 Hedonic Engine, the pricing core of the Hedonix platform.

title: The Boiling Pot: A Thought Experiment on Humanity's Horizon

detail.title: The Boiling Pot: A Thought Experiment on Humanity's Horizon
detail.abstract:
This essay examines what the structure of the human situation implies about humanity's trajectory across long timescales. The analysis proceeds from four minimal descriptive premises — plurality of social hierarchies, participant rather than authorial status with respect to physical reality, variation in disposition among hierarchy-leading minds, and a long horizon under triple mortality (individual, hierarchical, and civilizational) — and derives their consequences under explicit necessary conditions. Four derivations establish that any self-destruction capacity physics permits will eventually be developed somewhere within the union of hierarchies; that across long horizons at least one capacity-holder will reach a personal defeat moment with such capacity in hand; that triggering events propagate through cascade dynamics across the remaining capacity-holders; and that cumulative probability of cascade approaches unity unless suppression mechanisms scale faster than capacity emergence. 

A central analytical contribution is the diagnosis of the authorship illusion in strategic discourse — the implicit claim that dominant actors hold authorial status while addressing other actors as participants who must comply. The illusion is shown to be performatively self-refuting (asserted through talk rather than action), structurally self-eliminating across long horizons, internally incoherent on the actor's own principles when applied universally (the within / between contradiction), and operationally responsible for converting Dark Forest dynamics from hypothesis into practice through repeated demonstrations that erode the operational expectations of watching hierarchies. The analysis distinguishes unwisdom under actual superiority from strategic stupidity under merely perceived superiority, and develops a provisional taxonomy of decision orientations through which the framework's central question can be analytically engaged. 

The essay is forward-looking in perspective, conducted from the standpoint of a civilization currently approaching the entry-level natural selection filter the framework identifies. It does not predict outcomes; it makes structural pressures visible and leaves the central forecast as a genuinely open question for the reader. A companion essay takes the complementary backward-looking perspective. The framework offers no prescription. It claims only that these are the questions the long horizon forces upon any civilization that takes its own structural situation seriously.

title: The Architecture of Character: On the Virtues of a Self-Governing People

detail.title: The Architecture of Character: On the Virtues of a Self-Governing People
detail.abstract: This treatise constitutes the philosophical capstone of a trilogy on the principles of a free society. Where the preceding volumes constructed the political and economic architecture of liberty, this work confronts the question on which all such architecture rests: what character of citizen is required to inhabit and sustain a free republic? The central thesis holds that a free republic and a paternalistic administrative state are not merely competing systems of governance but competing ecosystems that cultivate two mutually exclusive types of citizen. The free republic, with its emphasis on individual sovereignty and personal responsibility, requires and fosters self-reliant, prudent, and courageous individuals; the administrative state, with its promise to insulate citizens from risk and guarantee outcomes, systematically engineers dependency, short-sightedness, and learned helplessness. Drawing on Cicero's virtus, Tocqueville's warning against "soft despotism," and Pennsylvania's historical experiment in self-governance under William Penn, the treatise examines the four foundational republican virtues — self-reliance, prudence, courage, and benevolence — and argues that their cultivation is the most powerful and sustainable form of resistance to administrative-state expansion. Successive chapters address education as character formation, the family as the first school of virtue, and civil society's "little platoons" as the architecture through which a self-governing people make the paternalistic state irrelevant. The work concludes that the project of liberty is never finished: it must be renewed by each generation through the deliberate cultivation of individual character.`

title: Has the Music Changed? Learning Financial Regimes from Continuous Wavelet Representations

detail.title: Has the Music Changed? Learning Financial Regimes from Continuous Wavelet Representations
detail.abstract:
Can multiscale spectral structure captured by Continuous Wavelet Transforms (CWT) enhance unsupervised financial regime detection, and does any such benefit depend on model architecture? We study this question under a deliberately challenging setting: the log-ratio of CCC-to-Single-A-rated option-adjusted spreads, a narrow, contested signal for which the credit-to-equity relationship is empirically ambiguous (Hilscher et al., 2015; Forte and Peña, 2009). We do this alongside a cross-domain replication experiment on CBOE’s Volatility Index (VIX), which represents a structurally distinct volatility process. Daily observations are transformed via the continuous wavelet transform into 450-dimensional time-frequency power representations and evaluated across geometric clustering (K-Means, DBSCAN/K-Means) and deep neural clustering (VAE, DEC) under multi-split walk-forward designs, transaction-cost constraints, and cross-signal replication.

Three broad findings emerge: 

First, spectral preprocessing improves neural regime detection consistently across signals but provides no systematic benefit to geometric clustering, establishing a strongly architecture-dependent effect (neural methods record 20/20 CWT-vs-raw sign-test wins on Sharpe, p = 10⁻⁶, while the neural-versus-geometric contrast is significant at p < 10⁻⁵). The evidence suggests multiscale information adds value only when the learning architecture can exploit it.

Second, the recovered spectral regimes exhibit economic content beyond statistical partitioning. Regime transitions imply differentiated 63-day conditional equity returns, while model entropy rises significantly during NBER recessions (t = 25.57, p < 0.0001) with a median lead of roughly 60 days. Importantly, the framework also distinguishes recessionary stress from several major post-2010 non-recessionary credit disturbances, suggesting relevance not only for historical crisis structure but for interpreting contemporary episodes of market stress.

Third, replication on VIX indicates the result is not signal-specific and clarifies the mechanism. Raw neural models deteriorate under fragmented walk-forward designs, whereas their CWT counterparts remain stable, consistent with spectral preprocessing acting as a structural regulariser. Once implementation frictions are considered, the economic contrast strengthens further: a high-turnover raw-feature benchmark is net negative in every configuration tested, while the spectral-neural methods remain strongly positive after transaction costs.

Rather than proposing a new forecasting model, the paper shows that continuous wavelet representations, when coupled with neural clustering, recover more persistent, economically coherent, and implementation-robust regime structure than raw-feature approaches on the same data.

title: The Human as Productive Input in AI-Driven Economies A New Foundation for the Taxation of Artificial Intelligence

detail.title: The Human as Productive Input in AI-Driven Economies A New Foundation for the Taxation of Artificial Intelligence
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a new conceptual foundation for the fiscal treatment of artificial intelligence in advanced economies. As AI substitutes human labor or enables disproportionate productive amplification, the wage channel through which solvent demand has historically been reproduced begins to weaken structurally. Existing fiscal proposals — robot taxes, heavier capital taxation, data dividends — address fragments of this problem but lack a unifying principle.

The central thesis recasts the human being as a productive input in AI-driven economies, but in a different position than before: not primarily as worker, but as the holder of solvent demand — the necessary condition for any market in which automated production can realize economic value. Classical factor theory characterizes a productive factor by three properties: necessity, scarcity, and identifiable ownership. Solvent demand in an AI-intensive economy satisfies all three. There is therefore no categorical obstacle to treating it as a productive factor in the classical sense, and access to that factor — long treated as a free good by firms extracting value from the market — must be reconsidered.

From this principle the paper derives three coherent instruments. The Market Access Tax (MAT) is levied on firms that extract value from solvent demand without compensatory contribution to its reproduction. The Market Access Right (MAR) is a border adjustment functionally analogous to the European Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism, but oriented to demand-factor leakage rather than carbon leakage. The Market Access Dividend (MAD) is a regular transfer to citizens, operationally similar to a universal basic income but resting on a different conceptual foundation: compensation for the role of holder of the demand factor, not redistribution.

The MAT/MAD architecture unifies the revenue and the expenditure sides under a single conceptual logic — structurally analogous to a sovereign-wealth scheme in which the underlying asset is the demand factor and the citizens are its collective holders. This distinguishes the proposal from generalized consumption taxes coupled with independently calibrated transfers (Korinek and Lockwood). It also differs from Korinek and Stiglitz (2025) in its starting point: rather than orienting innovation toward labor-complementing technologies, the framework accepts substitution as the likely trajectory and concentrates on the fiscal architecture required to redistribute its surplus without slowing it down.

Operationally, the MAT base combines two dimensions — direct displacement of human employment relative to a sectoral reference, and disproportionate AI-driven productive amplification. The second is measured through three convergent layers: direct technical metrics (tokens, GPU-hours), indirect economic inference relative to sectoral benchmarks, and a legally anchored enterprise declaration. This three-layer architecture is designed to remain resilient as the AI ecosystem evolves and individual metrics lose reliability. A non-braking calibration condition built into the instrument itself ensures that AI adoption remains economically attractive after the tax. Administration relies on coordination between two existing institutions — illustrated through the Italian case of INPS and the Agenzia delle Entrate — rather than the creation of a new agency.

The MAT is presented as a transitional instrument: a bridge, not a permanent end-state, designed to cushion the move from a wage-based to a post-wage distributive architecture, and to be integrated, in a longer horizon, into a broader regime of shared abundance should AI generate sustained material surplus. The framework forms part of a broader research program (IRIS — Initiative for Resilience and Social Inclusion), which also explores complementary monetary-fiscal architectures, including the Social Digital Bond (SDB) as a hypothesis under development.

title: The Sinkhole Trap: Rational Lock-In, Coercive Architecture, and the Failure of Revealed Preference as a Welfare Signal

detail.title: The Sinkhole Trap: Rational Lock-In, Coercive Architecture, and the Failure of Revealed Preference as a Welfare Signal
detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Sinkhole Trap, a theory describing how public infrastructure investment creates conditions under which private actors become rationally and inescapably locked into perpetual capital reinvestment cycles. The theory identifies a four-stage mechanism - entry with experiential opacity, deepening lock-in through coercive architecture, rational reinvestment at end of asset life, and active defence against stranding - that operates across transport infrastructure, energy systems, cloud computing, and housing markets.

The Sinkhole Trap's most significant implication concerns welfare economics methodology. Revealed preference is a valid inference mechanism only when the feasible choice set is exogenous to the policy being evaluated. The Sinkhole Trap identifies a specific structural class of cases in which this requirement fails; the policy itself endogenously constructs the choice set and its exit costs, rendering observed behaviour an unreliable welfare signal.

title: Post-Mortem Data in Infrastructure-Based Governance Systems

detail.title: Post-Mortem Data in Infrastructure-Based Governance Systems
detail.abstract:
Contemporary debates on post-mortem data governance treat regulatory failure as a problem of missing consent, unresolved digital inheritance, or inadequate extension of privacy rights beyond death. This paper rejects that diagnosis. It argues that in Global South, states organised around large scale Digital Public Infrastructure, post-mortem data governance fails for a different and more structural reason. Governance in such systems is infrastructural before it is constitutional. 
Drawing on India's population scale identity, welfare, financial, and data infrastructures, the paper shows that DPI systems are designed for permanence, accumulation, and interoperability. These systems routinely outlive the legal subject and continue to operate across administrative and algorithmic domains after death.
The paper critically examines three dominant approaches in existing scholarship: privacy extension beyond death, property and inheritance based models, and data stewardship or fiduciary frameworks. It demonstrates that all three fail in DPI centric Global South states for the same reason. Each assumes that regulatory legitimacy flows from individual agency. This assumption is untenable where access to rights, welfare, and public services is mediated through infrastructures that do not permit meaningful exit and do not recognise death as a governance endpoint.
Post-mortem data no longer functions as a residual personal interest, but as infrastructural surplus whose regulatory value emerges precisely from its detachment from contestation, withdrawal, and legal personality. By analysing post-mortem data as a diagnostic site, the paper exposes how infrastructural systems exercise public power without corresponding constitutional limits. 
The paper argues that effective regulation in DPI-heavy states requires a shift away from extending individual rights beyond death. It calls instead for public law constraints on infrastructural data power, including purpose limitation for postmortem retention, temporal justification requirements, and institutional accountability mechanisms capable of disciplining data governance where the legal subject no longer exists.

title: Information Linkages Across Developed, Emerging, and Frontier Equity Markets: Evidence from Implied Volatility
affiliations: North University of China, Macquarie University, Macquarie University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Information Linkages Across Developed, Emerging, and Frontier Equity Markets: Evidence from Implied Volatility
detail.abstract: This study examines whether forward-looking volatility reveals information linkages among developed, emerging, and frontier equity markets, and how these linkages changed during the COVID-19 pandemic. The analysis uses daily returns and ninety-day at-the-money implied volatilities for three exchange-traded funds representing developed (URTH), emerging (EEM), and frontier (FM) markets from October 2015 to November 2024. Information linkages are estimated using the generalized method of moments (GMM) framework of Fleming, Kirby, and Ostdiek (2001), complemented by ordinary least squares regressions and Monte Carlo simulations to test whether observed correlations exceed those expected from persistence alone. The results show strong cross-market linkages in forward-looking volatility. Daily log implied volatility correlations are approximately 59% between frontier and developed markets, 56% between frontier and emerging markets, and 80% between emerging and developed markets. Observed explanatory power is substantially higher than simulated thresholds, indicating that these correlations reflect genuine information transmission rather than spurious persistence. The GMM results confirm significant but incomplete information sharing across markets. Further analysis shows that the COVID-19 period significantly strengthened the linkage between frontier and emerging markets, while effects for other market pairs are weaker and statistically imprecise. Overall, the findings suggest that forward-looking volatility captures meaningful information flows across global equity markets and that global shocks can intensify linkages, particularly among less developed markets. These results highlight the importance of monitoring cross-market volatility linkages for risk management and policy coordination.

title: Beyond Algorithms: The Strategic Impact of Machine Learning on Modern Banking

detail.title: Beyond Algorithms: The Strategic Impact of Machine Learning on Modern Banking
detail.abstract: This research paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the implementation of machine learning (ML) in the banking and financial sectors. The primary objectives are to examine how ML enhances credit risk assessment, improves fraud detection and prevention, optimizes portfolio management and investment strategies, and personalizes customer services. Through a systematic review of existing literature and a methodological framework involving quantitative and qualitative analysis, this study identifies current trends, challenges, and gaps in ML adoption. The findings reveal that while ML offers transformative potential, issues such as data privacy, model interpretability, and integration with legacy systems remain significant hurdles. The paper concludes with recommendations for future research and practical implementations to bridge these gaps.

title:
World Liberty Financial: From Predicted Risks to Proven Realities
A 2024–2026 Case Study of Governance Failure, Liquidity Extraction, and Regulatory Conflict in Political DeFi

detail.title:
World Liberty Financial: From Predicted Risks to Proven Realities
A 2024–2026 Case Study of Governance Failure, Liquidity Extraction, and Regulatory Conflict in Political DeFi
detail.abstract: In October 2024, this author published a series of critical examinations of World Liberty Financial (WLFI), a governance token launched with the involvement of the Trump family, warning of concentrated ownership, non-transferable token structures, conflicts of interest, and the potential for exploitation. In April 2026, those warnings were fully realized. This paper documents the convergence between those early predictions and current events, including the token's 83% collapse to an all-time low, the use of WLFI tokens as collateral to borrow $150 million in stablecoins from a lending protocol co-founded by a WLFI advisor, a 93% utilization rate that trapped retail depositors, and a public investor revolt led by Justin Sun, who alleges that WLFI secretly embedded a backdoor blacklist function allowing unilateral asset freezes. Drawing on onchain data, regulatory filings, congressional correspondence, and investigative reporting, this paper argues that WLFI represents a case study in how political branding can mask structural deficiencies in DeFi governance. The paper concludes with policy recommendations for enhanced transparency, conflict-of-interest restrictions, and mandatory smart-contract disclosures for politically affiliated digital assets.

title: Household Vulnerability and Welfare Dynamics in Post-Conflict South Sudan: A Cross-Sectional Econometric Analysis

detail.title: Household Vulnerability and Welfare Dynamics in Post-Conflict South Sudan: A Cross-Sectional Econometric Analysis
detail.abstract: This study examines the determinants of household welfare in post-conflict South Sudan using cross-sectional econometric analysis of 3,550 households across six states and 50 enumeration areas in 2015. In a context where over 80% of the population lives in poverty following decades of conflict, understanding vulnerability-welfare relationships becomes critical for effective policy intervention. Employing state fixed effects models with cluster-robust standard errors, we identify statistically significant vulnerability effects on household welfare outcomes, with vulnerable households experiencing welfare scores 10.97 percentage points lower than those of non-vulnerable households (t-statistic = 31.98). The analysis reveals important asset-vulnerability interactions, with the negative impact of vulnerability diminishing as household asset levels increase, suggesting compound disadvantages for asset-poor vulnerable households. Robustness checks, including bootstrap validation, alternative clustering approaches, and different welfare measures, confirm the consistency of core findings across specifications. Policy targeting simulations indicate potential efficiency gains of 20% through improved welfare-based targeting mechanisms compared to current vulnerability-based approaches. Optimal targeting achieves 100% efficiency at 10% coverage, whereas current methods reach 85.7% efficiency. Heterogeneous effects analysis reveals that vulnerability impacts vary significantly across asset groups, with high-asset households showing the strongest vulnerability effects.

title: The False Promise of Public Benefit: Unmasking the 75 Countries Immigration Pause
affiliations: New York University School of Law

detail.title: The False Promise of Public Benefit: Unmasking the 75 Countries Immigration Pause
detail.abstract: On January 14, 2026, the Department of State announced a sweeping, indefinite pause on all immigrant visa issuances for nationals of 75 countries, effective January 21, 2026, premised upon a blanket presumption that applicants from these nations represent a high risk of becoming public charges. This Article argues that the pause is unlawful and should be set aside under the APA standard on multiple independent grounds. First, the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) affirmatively mandates individualized visa adjudication and prohibits categorical nationality-based bans of the kind the Department has imposed. Second, the consular nonreviewability doctrine — routinely invoked by the government as a shield — is structurally inapplicable here because the policy suppresses rather than reflects individual consular discretion. Third, robust public charge screening tools already exist and require case-by-case assessment. Fourth, the blanket pause cannot logically extend to self-sufficient visa categories such as EB-5, EB-2 NIW, and EB-1A. Fifth, the Department has failed to satisfy even the minimal reasoned explanation demanded by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), a bar that is now higher following the Supreme Court's elimination of Chevron deference in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo. Sixth, the pause is functionally final agency action. Seventh, if the executive branch wishes to reduce immigration from certain countries, the constitutional avenue runs through Congress, not the State Department. Eighth, this policy is not a Presidential Proclamation under INA § 212(f) and thus cannot claim the deference courts have extended to executive proclamations. This Article then proceeds to systematically refute the government's sur-reply in Storie v. Trump, No. 1:26-cv-00567 (D.D.C.), demonstrating that the government's 'containment strategy' fails on the merits, on the law, and in the face of documented human harm. Ninth, even if Trump v. CASA, Inc. (2025) restricts a district court's authority to issue universal preliminary injunctions under the general equitable power of the Judiciary Act of 1789, it does not foreclose the APA's own mandatory remedial provision. Under 5 U.S.C. § 706(2), a reviewing court shall 'hold unlawful and set aside' unlawful agency action — a statutory remedy that operates as vacatur with erga omnes effect, extending to all persons, not merely the named plaintiffs. The CASA majority expressly declined to resolve 'the distinct question whether the [APA] authorizes federal courts to vacate federal agency action,' and Justice Kavanaugh's concurrence confirmed that district courts may 'preliminarily set aside or decline to set aside an agency rule under the APA.' Because the Department of State is unambiguously an 'agency' within the meaning of the APA — unlike the President, who is not — the § 706(2) set-aside mechanism applies in full and is available to District Courts.

title: Why Gas Stations Charge Different Prices in the Same Area

detail.title: Why Gas Stations Charge Different Prices in the Same Area
detail.abstract: Gasoline prices often vary slightly between gas stations located in the same area, even though they sell the same product. This paper examines why these small price differences exist using real-world price data and basic microeconomic concepts. Data was collected from local gas stations using sources such as GasBuddy. The analysis shows that while prices are very similar due to competition, small differences still occur based on location, cost differences, and consumer behavior. Overall, the market is highly competitive but not perfectly uniform. Gasoline is a necessity for most consumers, especially in areas where driving is required for daily activities. Even though gas stations often operate close to each other and sell the same type of fuel, prices are not always identical. This raises an important economic question: why do gas stations in the same area charge different prices? Understanding this issue helps explain how real-world markets function and how businesses make pricing decisions. It also shows that even in markets that seem very competitive, small differences can still exist. This paper explores the reasons behind these price differences, focusing on factors such as competition, location, costs, and consumer behavior. This paper uses several key microeconomic concepts, including supply and demand, price elasticity of demand, and market competition. Supply and demand explain how the overall price of gasoline is determined in the market. title: The Impact of Taxes On Sugary Drink Consumption

From data sources such as FRED and personal reflection, the portrayal of growing lack of consumption begins to be more apparent.

detail.abstract: The current international monetary system is heavily influenced by dominant reserve currencies, particularly the US dollar, which creates structural imbalances in global trade and financial dependence among nations. This paper proposes the Malla Neutral Currency Model (MNCM), a conceptual framework for a neutral global currency used exclusively for international trade settlements and reserve holdings. The model does not replace national currencies but operates as a parallel system to facilitate trade neutrality. MNCM introduces a flexible, demand-supply-driven valuation mechanism where exchange relationships are determined individually between countries based on trade flows, economic conditions, and participation levels. Governance is designed as a hybrid structure combining equal country representation with trade-weighted influence. The model emphasizes decentralized adjustment, distributed responsibility, and behavioral incentives that encourage export-oriented economic balance.

title: The Policy Interest Rate Simulator: A Game-Based Approach for Teaching Monetary Policy
affiliations: Simon Fraser University (SFU) and University of British Columbia (UBC)

detail.title: The Policy Interest Rate Simulator: A Game-Based Approach for Teaching Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: This article introduces the Policy Interest Rate Simulator (PIRS) game, designed to help students understand the effects of central bank decisions on interest rates within a simulated economy. In the game, students play the role of a central bank, repeatedly setting policy interest rates. These decisions influence inflation and unemployment over time, while random events add unpredictability, making each playthrough dynamic and engaging. PIRS provides a hands-on, accessible approach for economics students to explore monetary policy and its implications. Players receive real-time feedback on the outcomes of their policy interest rate decisions, making it a valuable tool for both classroom use and independent learning. By simulating real-world central banking processes, the game helps students understand monetary policy and encourages critical discussions about policy decisions. It can also support classroom debates on central bank mandates, such as the U.S. Federal Reserve's dual mandate to promote maximum employment and stable prices, versus New Zealand's single mandate to maintain price stability.

detail.abstract: In this review, I focus on recent work that applies machine learning across domains in economics, finance, and healthcare. Drawing on over one hundred papers, I highlight how these domains address challenges related to regulatory transparency, temporal information leakage, algorithmic fairness, and the measurement of latent concepts. Although the papers discussed in my review are each unique and technical in their own right, there are important relationships among their themes. Together, they establish a tension between predictive power and interpretability, reveal a growing use of language models less for prediction than as measurement instruments, and reflect a growing body of work that turns unstructured text into usable variables for economic and clinical research.

detail.title: Topic Area: Distribution of wealth Issue: Economic heterogeneity Report Question: What are the effects of relative economic heterogeneity on children's economic success later in life in Uzbekistan?
detail.abstract: This article investigates the effects of relative economic heterogeneity on children's economic success later in life in Uzbekistan. Economic heterogeneity-differences in income, assets, and access to opportunities-shapes children's educational attainment, social capital, self-esteem, and long-term economic prospects. The study uses a qualitative research design based on literature review, comparative analysis, and case study methods. It analyzes secondary data and reports from the International Monetary Fund, the Washington Center for Equitable Growth, and global wealth statistics from the Hurun Report. In addition, the article applies illustrative case studies of prominent business figures, including Alisher Usmanov and Iskandar Makhmudov, to compare global and local patterns of social mobility. The findings suggest that although individual effort and talent contribute to success, access to quality education, parental investment, social networks, and broader economic conditions significantly influence long-term outcomes. The article concludes that reducing corruption, improving access to education, and implementing targeted economic empowerment programs are necessary to decrease inequality and enhance social mobility in Uzbekistan.

title: Ghost Statistics and Gender: A comparative assessment of fabricated and misrepresented statistics in men's and women's policy advocacy.
affiliations: , , affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Ghost Statistics and Gender: A comparative assessment of fabricated and misrepresented statistics in men's and women's policy advocacy.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Conflict of Interest: The authors declare no financial or institutional conflicts of interest

detail.abstract: Ghost statistics - fabricated, misattributed, or systematically misrepresented numerical claims - have become a persistent feature of contemporary policy discourse. This paper presents a comparative assessment of ghost statistics across men's and women's policy advocacy domains, examining their origins, institutional reach, policy impact, debunking visibility, and lifespan after formal correction across multiple geographic and cultural contexts including North America, Europe, and the Global South. Drawing on Joel Best's foundational framework for the social construction of statistics, we analyse eight documented ghost statistics spanning workplace equity, criminal justice, health, family structure, international development, and press freedom. Our central methodological contribution is twofold. First, we introduce the concept of the contaminated evidence chain- the risk that secondary sources used to establish advocacy baselines may themselves carry the evidentiary deficiencies under investigation - and articulate explicit disciplinary commitments for managing this risk. Second, we address the compensation argument directly: that dedicated international institutions for women's issues (UN Women, CEDAW, the series of World Conferences on Women) exist as warranted compensatory responses to documented historical exclusion and therefore cannot be cited as evidence of preferential advocacy treatment. We accept the historical premise fully while demonstrating that it does not resolve the normalization problem, because institutional compensation and downstream structural consequences for ghost statistic production are logically independent phenomena. Our analysis finds that ghost statistics exist in both advocacy domains at broadly comparable rates when normalized against advocacy activity. The principal asymmetry is not in prevalence but in trajectory, a finding we term the correction asymmetry gap. Ghost statistics associated with women's issues achieve substantially higher policy impact, amplified through heads of state, UN bodies, and major international funders. Ghost statistics associated with men's issues demonstrate greater longevity and markedly lower correction visibility, persisting in public discourse with minimal formal challenge. Both dynamics cause harm to the communities they purport to serve. The paper concludes that statistical literacy reform is essential across all advocacy contexts regardless of the justice of the underlying cause, and that the correction asymmetry gap represents a structural feature of gendered advocacy environments warranting systematic attention.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we show that using multiple models when executing a specific task almost unavoidably gives rise to interaction between them, especially when their number is large. We show that this interaction can lead to biased and incomplete results if treated inappropriately (which we believe is the current standard in the financial industry). We propose the use of Probabilistic Graphical Models - a machine learning technique as a remedy to this problem. We discuss some numerical aspects of our approach that will be present in any practical implementation. We then examine, in detail, a practical example of using this method in a stress testing context.

title: Economics from First Principles: The Ontology, Morality, and Logic of Liberty

detail.title: Economics from First Principles: The Ontology, Morality, and Logic of Liberty
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified first-principles account of liberty by grounding economics, law, and political order in Natural Law. Through a sustained Socratic dialogue, it demonstrates that self-ownership, private property acquired by honest labor, and the non-aggression principle follow directly from three ontological pillars-genuine free will, objective universal truth, and fixed rational human nature-that are themselves most coherently explained by the teleological design of a good Creator. These foundations render any institution claiming the right to initiate force (the State) intrinsically immoral, while simultaneously establishing libertarianism as the only moral framework fully consistent with human nature and the only practical framework capable of solving the knowledge, calculation, and coordination problems that doom central planning. Markets, under secure property rights and voluntary exchange, generate emergent order, widespread prosperity, and genuine virtue precisely because they align with man's created telos; coercive redistribution, regulation, and social engineering fight that telos and therefore produce poverty, resentment, and tyranny. A supporting Christian cultural matrix--emphasizing individual dignity, truth-telling, voluntary charity, and suspicion of concentrated power--is shown to be the historical and practical soil in which such liberty endures. The paper concludes with a candid diagnosis of America's departure from these principles, and appends rigorous responses to market-failure objections together with proposed constitutional safeguards to entrench the ontological foundations and strictly cabin any minimal-state exceptions. Throughout, the argument upholds that true liberty arises not from human invention but from alignment with the moral and ontological order of reality itself.

title: The Statistical Validation Problem in Financial Cycle Detection

detail.title: The Statistical Validation Problem in Financial Cycle Detection

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder of FractalCycles, a quantitative analytics platform that operationalizes statistical cycle validation across financial instruments and timeframes. This paper is a methodological position paper that consolidates primary-source references from outside finance. It does not promote any specific FractalCycles feature or pricing tier, and it does not propose a new test. The author has no other relationships, financial or otherwise, that could be perceived as having influenced this work.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This is a methodology survey paper that uses only published references. No human or animal subjects are involved.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded by FractalCycles Research. No external grants or sponsorships.

detail.abstract: Apparent cycles emerge in any sufficiently long financial price series, including pure random walks. This paper surveys the statistical validation problem at the heart of cycle detection: distinguishing periodicity that arises from genuine market structure from periodicity that arises by chance under a null hypothesis of independent or short-range-dependent returns. We review three canonical tools imported into finance from older disciplines, namely Goertzel's narrowband discrete Fourier transform (Goertzel, 1958), Bartels' significance test (Bartels, 1935), and the Hurst exponent (Hurst, 1951), and we summarize the published evidence for and against their use as cycle filters in financial time series. We argue that detection without a strict null model is curve-fitting, and that the validation gap explains why so many published cycle claims fail out of sample. The paper does not propose a new test. It consolidates primary-source references into a framework that researchers, practitioners, and reviewers can use when evaluating future cycle claims, both academic and commercial.

title: Minimum Wage, Unemployment and Macroeconomic Fluctuations: Evidence from Puerto Rico

detail.title: Minimum Wage, Unemployment and Macroeconomic Fluctuations: Evidence from Puerto Rico

publicationDetails.detailsText: This paper was accepted on March 19, 2025, to appear in an upcoming edition of the CEPAL Review.

detail.abstract: This study evaluates how the United States (US) federal minimum wage impacts Puerto Rico's (PR) unemployment rate, using a structural model to analyze dynamic shocks in aggregate demand and supply using quarterly data from 2001 to 2019. For robustness and consistency, we employ a combined approach. First, we apply a structural vector autoregressive (SVAR) model to establish causality and assess the real dynamic effects and fiscal shocks from minimum wage increases, complemented by an autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) bounds testing framework. The impulse-response functions suggest that the minimum wage has a short-term negative effect on unemployment, with the peak occurring in the second quarter, implying that the labor market undergoes a readjustment process. The possibility of the minimum wage reducing unemployment offers a unique perspective, especially in Puerto Rico's context. According to the ARDL model, it takes approximately three months for variables to reach long-run equilibrium, with the minimum wage's lasting impact on unemployment statistically significant at 1%.

title: Airport pricing and capacity with non-aviation markets: single-till versus dual-till regulation
affiliations: Osaka University of Economics - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Airport pricing and capacity with non-aviation markets: single-till versus dual-till regulation

declarations.funderStatement: The financial support received from JSPS KAKENHI (Grant Number 24K04878) is gratefully acknowledged.

detail.abstract: This study investigates airport pricing and runway capacity in the presence of non-aviation markets to evaluate the relative performance of single-till versus dual-till regulations implemented at public airports for cost recovery. Using general and specified functional approaches, we obtain the following results. First, when the profits from the non-aviation market are exogenously given and positive, single-till regulation achieves higher social welfare than dual-till regulation. Second, when non-aviation profits are endogenously determined, dual-till (single-till) regulated airports generate negative (positive) profits from that market. Third, given this negative profit property, dual-till regulation achieves higher (lower) social welfare than single-till regulation when the complementarity between aviation and nonaviation demands is high (low). Fourth, both dual-till and single-till regulated airports overinvest in runway capacity, although dual-till regulated airports overinvest less (more) when demand complementarity is high (low). These clear-cut results provide important policy implications for regulatory authorities concerned with public interests.

title: Bridging the Is-Ought Gap: Foundational Normative Assumptions, Human Flourishing, and the Advantages of Theistic Natural Law

detail.title: Bridging the Is-Ought Gap: Foundational Normative Assumptions, Human Flourishing, and the Advantages of Theistic Natural Law
detail.abstract: The is-ought gap, first articulated by David Hume in 1739, poses a persistent challenge in meta-ethics: no set of purely descriptive premises can logically entail a normative conclusion without the addition of at least one foundational normative assumption. Any coherent defense of liberty, self-ownership, private property acquired by honest labor, and the non-aggression principle must rest upon three ontological pillars-genuine free will and moral responsibility, objective universal truth, and fixed rational human nature. This paper examines the logical structure of the gap and surveys the major foundational normative assumptions that have been invoked to bridge it: theistic Natural Law (with its operative anthropology of rational dignity), Aristotelian eudaimonism, Kantian rational agency, non-natural moral realism, and constructivist/contractarian approaches. Each assumption is evaluated according to how well it supports, coheres with, or stands in tension with these three ontological pillars. A dedicated analysis further reveals how progressive pedagogical traditions have systematically undermined these pillars by attenuating the second act of the intellect (judgment) and shifting the operative anthropology from one of responsible moral agency to a malleable managed resource-a process exemplified by the dominant implicit assumption in contemporary US public education: a hybrid of secular constructivism, expressive individualism, and managerial progressivism that treats human nature as plastic and the good as socially constructed through expert consensus and equity metrics. Despite their surface differences, all frameworks converge on human flourishing as the ultimate evaluative criterion. Given this shared telos, the dependence of liberty upon secure ontological foundations, and the cultural and educational mechanisms required to transmit them, the paper argues that a theistic Natural Law framework centered on a benevolent intelligent designer provides the most coherent, stable, and empirically robust foundation for the institutions of liberty and the greatest attainable expansion of measurable human flourishing. It uniquely unifies ontology and axiology, supplies the deepest metaphysical grounding for the three pillars, and has historically generated the cultural and educational matrix most conducive to secure property rights, generalized trust, and sustained prosperity.

title: Kinshasa and Climate Change: How Population Growth Exacerbates Vulnerability

detail.title: Kinshasa and Climate Change: How Population Growth Exacerbates Vulnerability

detail.abstract: Kinshasa's climate vulnerability stems not solely from climate change but from the convergence of sustained population growth (≈ 4%/year), unplanned urbanization, and the intensification of hydrological extremes. This article examines three amplification mechanisms: population concentration in areas of maximum hydrological risk; erosion of collective adaptive capacity; and-a plausible but quantitatively uncertain contributor-deforestation for housing and energy. The article rigorously distinguishes between two distinct hydrological events: the torrential rains and landslides of December 12-13, 2022, in Mont-Ngafula and Ngaliema (≥ 169 official deaths; indicative range 220-305 when applying an underreporting factor of 1.3-1.8), and the exceptional flooding of the Congo River in late December 2023-January 2024 (≈ 6.20 m, approaching the 1961 record of 6.26 m). The analysis links a critical framework-land governance as a structural mediator-to an illustrative heuristic representation ("vulnerability scissors") and three prospective pathways to 2050. An operational framework under political conditions is proposed around four pillars, at an indicative cost of $4.5-8 billion over 20 years-a scale of magnitude that, when compared to the annual budget of the City-Province of Kinshasa (≈ $200-400 million), reveals the central challenge of concessional and climate financing. Without a transformation of the urban political economy in the decade 2026-2035, Kinshasa and comparable humid-tropical megacities will face increasing humanitarian disasters.

title: LiveFace: Real-Time Photorealistic Facial Animation on Low-End Mobile Devices via Compact Per-Avatar Neural Decoders and Universal Compositor-Upscaler

detail.title: LiveFace: Real-Time Photorealistic Facial Animation on Low-End Mobile Devices via Compact Per-Avatar Neural Decoders and Universal Compositor-Upscaler
detail.abstract: We present LiveFace, a modular neural rendering system that achieves photorealistic talking-head animation at 30 fps on low-end mobile devices with as little as ~10 GFLOPS of compute (e.g., Qualcomm Snapdragon 439). Prior photorealistic facial animation systems either require cloud infrastructure with 100M+ parameter models (HeyGen, DID , Synthesia) or demand desktop-class GPUs (MetaHuman, Audio2Face), while on-device alternatives sacrifice realism for stylized cartoon aesthetics (Apple Memoji, Samsung AR Emoji). LiveFace bridges this gap through three key contributions: (1) a decomposed per-avatar decoder architecture that factorizes the face into four independently rendered regions-mouth, eyes, hair, and body-each handled by a compact neural decoder (1.3-5.7M parameters) augmented with a 128-dimensional learnable identity embedding; (2) a universal compositor-upscaler (~7M parameters) shared across all avatars that composites the decoded patches onto a 9:16 portrait canvas and upscales to 360x640 (or 384x672) in a single forward pass; and (3) a videodriven knowledge distillation pipeline that uses RAVDESS emotional speech videos as driving sources for LivePortrait (~300M parameters) to generate diverse, naturalistic training data for the student decoders. The MouthDecoder supports dual-input conditioning: both viseme-based (audio-driven) and landmark-based (MediaPipe Face Mesh) modes, enabling flexible integration with different upstream pipelines. A perframe quality filter employing Haar cascade face detection, Laplacian blur scoring, and SSIM comparison ensures training data integrity by rejecting approximately 0.6% of generated frames. A working V3 prototype has been trained and validated, demonstrating that the architecture successfully produces photorealistic output from compact per-avatar models.

title: A Steep Climb: Financing Canada's NATO Commitment while Maintaining Fiscal Discipline
affiliations: C.D. Howe Institute and C.D. Howe Institute

detail.title: A Steep Climb: Financing Canada's NATO Commitment while Maintaining Fiscal Discipline
detail.abstract:
• Canada’s NATO commitment to raise defence spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035 will prompt a reshaping of federal finances. Defence spending will approach $150 billion by 2034/35, roughly triple current levels, and rival the annual amount of major transfers to provinces.
  • Under the status quo, higher defence spending would significantly increase deficits and put both the deficit-to-GDP and debt-to-GDP ratios on upward trajectories.
  • Weak productivity, slow economic growth, an ageing population, and high debt levels limit Canada’s ability to accommodate the NATO defence spending commitment without broader fiscal changes. Some combination of tax increases, spending cuts, or taking on more debt is required.
  • A mixed approach that combines a modest GST increase with slower growth in non-defence spending offers a practical path to meeting NATO commitments while maintaining fiscal sustainability, alongside clearer budget reporting on defence spending to track progress toward the target.

title: Using Large Language Models to Interpret Central Bank Speak
affiliations: , BlackRock, Inc, , BlackRock and BlackRock, Inc

detail.title: Using Large Language Models to Interpret Central Bank Speak
detail.abstract: Central bank communications move financial markets, but assessing policy stance at scale remains manual and time-intensive. Investors and policymakers need rapid, consistent judgments of whether minutes signal tighter (hawkish) or looser (dovish) policy, yet technical language and institutional nuance make automation difficult. We evaluate whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably classify monetarypolicy stance in central bank communications, benchmarking against expert labels from BlackRock macro specialists. We extend the existing literature by moving from single-institution studies to a cross-institution benchmark: we analyze 1,722 sentences from the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank, and Bank of England under a unified methodology, which allows us to distinguish model behavior that is consistent across institutions from patterns driven by institution-specific communication styles. Overall, LLM predictions closely track expert judgments, with disagreements largely confined to adjacent classes rather than polarity reversals. Models systematically under-use extreme categories relative to humans. Performance is highest for the Bank of England, consistent with experts assigning fewer extreme labels to BoE communications, which reduces the penalty from under-using extremes. As a robustness check, collapsing the five-class taxonomy to three classes (Dovish/Neutral/Hawkish) increases agreement while leaving the overall pattern of model performance similar; under this mapping, LLaMA-70B achieves 66% accuracy against expert labels. Under the five-class taxonomy, GPT-5 and LLaMA-70B perform best on the pooled sample across central banks, while another open-weight alternative, DeepSeek-R1, performs competitively with GPT-4o-supporting reproducible, scalable, near-real-time stance measurement without relying solely on closed models.

title: More Information, Less Power: Field Experimental Evidence on the Effect of Information Provision on Residential Electricity Consumption
affiliations: Energieinstitut at the Johannes Kepler Universität Linz, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: More Information, Less Power: Field Experimental Evidence on the Effect of Information Provision on Residential Electricity Consumption

declarations.ethicsApproval: An ethics review was conducted during the proposal check.
declarations.funderStatement: This project has received funding from the European Unions’s Horizon 2020 research and innovation programme under the grant agreement No. 695945.

detail.abstract: We study the causal effect of digital information provision on household electricity consumption using a randomized field experiment with a staggered rollout. Households were randomly assigned to an information condition (N = 449), receiving access to a smartphone application with feedback on electricity use, costs, emissions, social comparisons, and gamified learning features, or to a control condition (N = 443) without app access. We measure electricity consumption using high-frequency smart-meter data for up to 70 weeks after treatment. App access reduces daily electricity consumption by approximately 4.5--5%. The effect emerges within two weeks and remains statistically significant for roughly 20-25 weeks. Thereafter, consumption remains below the control group, but differences are no longer estimated precisely enough to reject zero.  App engagement declines sharply after rollout, and higher engagement is associated with larger and more persistent reductions in consumption. The findings suggest that digital feedback can reduce residential electricity demand, but that persistence depends on sustained user attention.

title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on College Students: A Study

detail.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence on College Students: A Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study does not involve human or animal subjects requiring ethical approval.

detail.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools in education has increased rapidly in recent years, and it has clearly changed the way university students study and complete their academic work. Tools like ChatGPT, Grammarly, and similar AI-based platforms are now commonly used by students to find information quickly, improve their writing, and finish assignments in less time. While these tools are helpful in increasing productivity, there are growing concerns about how they might affect students' critical thinking and overall understanding of concepts. In this study, an attempt has been made to understand how AI tools influence academic performance as well as cognitive development. It was observed that students often rely on these tools for completing tasks faster and producing well-structured work. In many cases, this leads to better academic results. However, at the same time, frequent use of AI tools can reduce the effort students put into thinking, analyzing, and solving problems on their own. From the overall analysis, it can be said that AI tools are useful if they are used in a controlled and meaningful way. But if students become too dependent on them, it may negatively affect their ability to think independently. Therefore, it is important to maintain a balance where AI is used as a support system rather than a complete replacement for human thinking.

title: NEPA's Midlife Crisis

detail.title: NEPA's Midlife Crisis

keywords: Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County

detail.abstract:
The National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) is in the throes of a midlife crisis. In just the last three years, Congress amended NEPA for the first time since 1970, the Supreme Court issued its first major NEPA decision in two decades, and the Council on Environmental Quality (CEQ) rescinded its NEPA implementing regulations. Taken together, these developments do not explicitly repeal NEPA, but they reallocate its action-forcing power away from a centralized federal procedural baseline and toward a proximate-cause limited exercise in expanded agency discretion.

This Article is among the first to situate this trifecta within longer, intersecting arcs. First, it traces NEPA’s doctrinal growing pains since Public Citizen, showing how lower courts’ two-decade struggle parsing indirect effects and causal responsibility set the jurisprudential groundwork for Congress’s 2023 amendments and the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Seven County Infrastructure Coalition v. Eagle County. Second, it lays bare the ongoing struggle between an apparent judicial skepticism of administrative authority and judicial deference to so-called expert agencies.

The Article proceeds in three Parts. Part I begins with NEPA’s Carson-era origins and federal leadership ambitions that reflected a national reckoning with the impacts of rapid industrialization and its unchecked externalities but also forecasted the statute’s eventual undoing. Part II chronicles NEPA’s implementation through the CEQ, hard-look review, circuit splits, and agency implementation. Part III evaluates NEPA’s amendments, Seven County’s deference and causation reminders, and the regulatory blowback culminating in CEQ’s regulation rescission. The central argument is that NEPA no longer serves as a reliable, national environmental conscience; its revival depends on a renewed political commitment to accountability akin to the awareness that enabled NEPA’s passage more than a half-century ago.

detail.abstract: This study reexamines the relationship between exports and economic growth in India by separating short-run dynamics from long-run equilibrium relationships. Set against India's shift from an inward-looking, state-led model to a liberalised and globally integrated economy, the analysis emphasises how trade structure and import dependence shape growth. Using quarterly data from 2005Q3-2025Q2 and the ARDL bounds testing approach, the study tests whether exports act as a sustained engine of growth. Results confirm stable long-run relationships among GDP, exports, and imports. However, exports do not show a positive long-run effect on growth; their association with GDP turns negative when imports are included. Imports, in contrast, have a positive and significant long-run impact, highlighting the role of imported capital goods, intermediate inputs, and energy in supporting productivity and capacity. In the short run, both exports and imports positively influence output, indicating that trade supports cyclical growth even if long-run drivers differ. Overall, India's growth appears more importsupported and domestically driven than export-led.

title: Persistent Homology of Stock Market Correlation Structure: Topological Detection of Stress Regimes in Equity Market

detail.title: Persistent Homology of Stock Market Correlation Structure: Topological Detection of Stress Regimes in Equity Market

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based exclusively on publicly available secondary data (historical stock prices and market indices). detail.abstract: This paper examines the applicability of persistent homology for detecting market stress regimes based on the correlation structure of the Russian stock market. For the 25 most liquid equities listed on the Moscow Exchange, spanning eight economic sectors over the period January 2014 - April 2026, a metric space is constructed using the Mantegna distance, and H1-homologies of the Vietoris-Rips filtration are computed on rolling windows. A two-scale topological structure is identified: during stress periods, correlation intransitivity increases at the high-correlation scale and decreases at the low-correlation scale. The proposed scale-specific indicator is a statistically significant predictor of stress-regime transitions in logistic regression, controlling for current volatility and standard correlation metrics; the sign of the relationship is robust to temporal cross-validation. On the test sample, the indicator with fixed scale boundaries is insignificant; however, shifting the boundaries toward higher correlations restores significance, indicating nonstationarity of the informative scale. Linear predictive ability for volatility levels is not found, confirming the suitability of topological methods for qualitative regime detection rather than quantitative forecasting. Decomposition of the topological signal to the level of specific stock triples and intersectoral links enables direct economic interpretation and real-time identification of intransitivity sources.

title: When do contingent valuation and discrete choice experiments converge? Evidence from a meta-analysis of environmental valuation studies
affiliations: Department of Agriculture, Food and Environment, University of Messina,  and Norwegian University of Life Sciences

detail.title: When do contingent valuation and discrete choice experiments converge? Evidence from a meta-analysis of environmental valuation studies

contentType.other: submitted paper to a journal for publication

detail.abstract: Understanding when different stated preference methods yield comparable welfare estimates remains a central issue in environmental valuation. This study provides a systematic meta-analytic assessment of when willingness-to-pay (WTP) estimates from contingent valuation (CV) and discrete choice experiments (DCE) converge, using 74 direct comparisons from 47 studies under strict comparability conditions. The analysis combines continuous meta-regression models with discrete-response specifications capturing the direction of divergence. The results are consistent with convergence in magnitude. On average, DCE and CV WTP estimates do not differ significantly. However, substantial heterogeneity across comparisons indicates that convergence reflects a central tendency rather than full equivalence. Within-sample comparisons are systematically associated with a lower likelihood that DCE yields higher WTP estimates than CV. This suggests that part of the observed gap may reflect differences in sample composition rather than purely methodological effects. Attribute complexity is positively associated with the DCE-CV gap, whereas the effect of task complexity is more conditional, with reductions in differences more evident in within-sample designs and in specifications that control for scale. The analysis further shows that proportional differences increase with the magnitude of WTP, consistent with scale heterogeneity. By contrast, the direction of differences is more context-dependent and less predictable. Overall, the findings show that convergence between DCE and CV is not a fixed property, but a conditional, design-dependent outcome shaped by interactions among survey design, sample comparability, and scale effects. Continuous measures of divergence provide more robust evidence than categorical classifications, supporting a gradual rather than discrete interpretation of differences between stated preference methods.

title: Systemic risk and financial contagion between the insurance and the banking sector in Morocco
affiliations: University Hassan II Casablanca and University Hassan II Casablanca

detail.title: Systemic risk and financial contagion between the insurance and the banking sector in Morocco
detail.abstract: This paper examines the link between systemic risk and financial contagion between the banking and insurance sectors in Morocco. It presents one of the first quantitative assessments of four major Moroccan financial firms, all listed on the Casablanca Stock Exchange, based on 952 weekly observations collected between October 2007 and December 2025. Using both the CoVaR model developed by Adrian and Brunnermeier (2016) and the contagion index model by Diebold and Yilmaz (2012), we demonstrate that, despite relatively low overall financial connectivity in Morocco, systemic risk exists in highly unbalanced directional channels, rather than being geographically dispersed across all entities. Furthermore, the total amount of systemic risk generated by Moroccan insurance companies (Δ CoVaR = -0.030) is higher than that generated by banks (Δ CoVaR = -0.021), which contradicts the literature’s definition that banking centrality is the predominant paradigm. Among the four firms, Wafa Assurance exhibits the highest transmission of systemic risk (122.36%) and a net contagion effect of +26.50% originating from the insurance sector (rather than banks). Furthermore, there is a significant contagion effect from the insurance sector to the banking sector. Following the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, systemic interconnections have increased compared to previous levels, with the overall value of the total contagion index standing at 65%, well above the level seen during the 2008 global financial crisis. There is therefore an urgent need to establish coordinated macroprudential regulation and supervision between the Insurance and Social Security Supervisory Authority (ACAPS) and Bank Al-Maghrib.
