This research was conducted independently and received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors."
declarations.ethicsApproval: "This study is purely theoretical and did Python-based conceptual analysis. It did not involve human participants, clinical trials, or the collection of sensitive personal data. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required."
declarations.funderStatement: NON

detail.abstract: This article constitutes a central component within the paradigm of Consciousness Flexibility (CF) developed by David Zinger, as elaborated in his SSRN research series. Within this paradigm, the article examines the concept of understanding in an era characterized by knowledge abundance and algorithmic mediation, arguing that the traditional relationship between knowledge and understanding has broken down. Whereas understanding was previously conceived as the result of accumulating and processing knowledge, knowledge is now often received as algorithmic output, whose conditions of production are not fully transparent.

title: The Capital Velocity Gap: A Multi-State Forensic Analysis of Innovation Funding Intermediaries in the Rust Belt

detail.title: The Capital Velocity Gap: A Multi-State Forensic Analysis of Innovation Funding Intermediaries in the Rust Belt
detail.abstract: State governments allocate substantial public revenue to foster entrepreneurship, typically via nonprofit 'innovation intermediaries' and state-backed venture capital programs. This paper introduces the Direct Capital Ratio (DCR)—the proportion of funding reaching founders as investment—as a metric for institutional efficiency. A forensic audit of intermediaries across the Rust Belt (PA, OH, MI, WI, IN) reveals a structural efficiency crisis: DCRs range from under 1% to 55%, with an average of approximately 27 cents reaching founders for every state dollar appropriated.

title: AI in Algorithmic Trading & Market Prediction

detail.title: AI in Algorithmic Trading & Market Prediction
detail.abstract: This paper examines the growing role of artificial intelligence in algorithmic trading and market prediction. The study is motivated by the rapid increase in financial data, the spread of automated trading systems, and the limits of traditional forecasting models when markets become nonlinear, volatile, and information-rich. Building on the initial project question, the paper reviews how machine learning, deep learning, reinforcement learning, and natural language processing are being used to generate trading signals, forecast short-term price movements, optimize execution, and support portfolio decisions. It also compares AI-based approaches with classical statistical frameworks such as regression, ARIMA, and volatility models. The review shows that AI can improve pattern recognition and adapt more quickly to changing data structures, especially when large structured and unstructured datasets are available. However, the literature also shows that forecasting success does not automatically translate into consistent abnormal returns once transaction costs, regime shifts, overfitting, and market impact are considered. To address these issues, the paper proposes a transparent empirical methodology based on walk-forward testing, benchmark comparison, and risk-adjusted evaluation. Overall, AI appears to be a powerful enhancement to algorithmic trading, but not a guaranteed replacement for sound financial theory, robust validation, and effective risk control.

title: The Political Sustainability of Fuel Subsidy Reform: Rent Appropriation versus Public Grievance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Technical University of Manabi, Catholic University of Santiago de Guayaquil and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Political Sustainability of Fuel Subsidy Reform: Rent Appropriation versus Public Grievance
detail.abstract: Fossil fuel subsidy reforms frequently provoke political resistance, including mass mobilizationand violent unrest. This study examines how different types of fuel price reforms influence protest dynamics in Ecuador, a case whose varied subsidy experiences reflect broader challenges facing many developing economies. Using a novel methodological approach that combines administrative police records with ACLED and GDELT protest indicators through neural networks and ARIMAX models, we construct a high-frequency daily protest-intensity index for the period from 2018 to 2023. A Vector Autoregressive (VAR) model is then used to test whether changes in diesel, regular, and premium gasoline prices Granger-cause shifts in protest activity and to simulate responses to sudden price shocks. The results reveal substantial heterogeneity: diesel price increases trigger significant and persistent protests, whereas regular gasoline hikes generate only modest, short-lived responses,and premium gasoline reforms have no significant impact. These patterns indicate that the rentappropriation mechanism, driven by concentrated economic losses among organized stakeholders, is a more critical driver of large-scale mobilization than the grievance pathway resulting from diffuse public hardship. By highlighting the pivotal roles of stakeholder structure and loss concentration, this study contributes to wider debates on distributive politics and the political economy of the energy transition. Finally, the findings provide empirically grounded guidance for policymakers seeking to design fuel subsidy reforms that balance fiscal sustainability and environmental imperatives with political stability.

title: Fuelwood use and ambient air pollution in urban central-southern Chile: Do poor and rich households contribute equally to this public bad?
affiliations: University of Concepción, University of Talca and University of Concepción

detail.title: Fuelwood use and ambient air pollution in urban central-southern Chile: Do poor and rich households contribute equally to this public bad?
detail.abstract: The combustion of fuelwood to produce energy is a major source of air pollution in developing and middle-income countries, negatively affecting the well-being of vulnerable populations. These effects contrast with individuals’ contributions to this problem, which often relate to their relative position in the income distribution. This paper pursues two objectives: first, to analyze the income and non-income drivers of fuelwood consumption at the extremes of the income distribution, accounting for the selection nature of fuelwood use; and second, to examine the spatial determinants of the share of fuelwood users at the communal level through spatial panel data models. Results suggest that the enactment of environmentally saturated areas is more effective in reducing consumption among high-income households, highlighting affordability constraints for the poor. Regarding the spatial analysis, spatial dependence is found to be a stronger determinant of fuelwood use among low-income households, while income exerts a greater influence among wealthier households, suggesting that targeted policies promoting energy transition among higher-income groups could substantially contribute to improving urban air quality.

title: A Model of Multidestination Trips: An application to commercial fishing and fuel policies
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and University of California

detail.title: A Model of Multidestination Trips: An application to commercial fishing and fuel policies
detail.abstract: Motivated by the gap between the existence of high-resolution spatial-temporal mobility data within trips and the lack of mechanistic models for within-trip behavior, we develop a micro-model of a multi-destination trip. The model incorporates simultaneous decisions on location choice, effort allocation, travel route, and trip length. While focused on commercial fishing, multi-destination trips are present in recreation and tourism, natural resource hunting and gathering, and transportation. We analytically demonstrate the interconnectedness between sites visited, route and effort allocation decisions, as well as how these decisions are contingent upon the underlying vessel capital. Calibrating the model to the U.S. Gulf of Mexico reef fisheries, we employ discrete-continuous optimization to determine the spatial patterns of forward-looking and myopic vessels. We find that vessel heterogeneity in terms of fishing capital and foresight produces distinct patterns of resource use, including site selection, effort distribution, and trip duration. We highlight the policy usefulness of the model by considering the distributional impacts of a fuel policy (tax or subsidy). We show that fuel policies may elicit trip-level behavioral responses, but whether there is one depends on a complex interaction between vessel capital, fishing production, and the relative magnitude of the policy. Our findings can help guide empirical assessments on the impacts of fuel policies on fishing capacity, patterns of resource use, changes in fuel use, emissions, and distributional effects across the fishing fleet.

title: The Green New Product Problem: growth or greenflation?

detail.title: The Green New Product Problem: growth or greenflation?
detail.abstract: Decarbonising modern economies requires the reconfiguration of almost every aspect of economic life. In public policy circles, there is widespread debate as to whether the development and adoption of green innovations is likely to accelerate growth over the short- to medium-term, or whether the net-zero agenda will constrain output and exacerbate inflationary pressures. This paper explores an often-overlooked aspect of this debate: namely, how judgements concerning the conceptualisation and classification of innovative green technologies by economists and national statistical authorities affect economic impact assessments and growth trajectories. It contests that failing to account properly for new green technologies can lead to an understatement of the growth benefits of the green transition in both economic models and real GDP metrics. Using the transition to electric vehicles as an example, the paper estimates that the rollout of novel green technologies could result in either a 17% increase in the contribution of these expenditures to real GDP growth or a 17% spike in their contribution to inflation over a ten-year period, depending on how national statistical authorities choose to conceptualise green innovations.

title: Smog, Not Lights. Tracking Bolivia's 2024-2026 Recession from Space
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN and AI Analytics

detail.title: Smog, Not Lights. Tracking Bolivia's 2024-2026 Recession from Space
detail.abstract: Nighttime lights are the standard satellite proxy for economic activity, but they fail to detect recessions. On a 2020-2024 panel of nine Bolivian departments, VIIRS lights match the sign of PIB growth 78 percent of the time during expansions but only 39 percent during contractionsworse than coin-flip. The reason is structural: lit infrastructure is a stock that does not contract when activity falls, while fossil-fuel combustion is a flow that does. Tropospheric NO 2 , a neardirect measure of combustion retrieved daily by ESA's Sentinel-5P satellite, maintains 72 percent sign concordance during contractions. We exploit this asymmetry to build a monthly recession indicator from TROPOMI NO 2 over eleven Bolivian metropolitan areas, July 2018 through April 2026. The indicator peaked in June 2023; INE quarterly PIB first registered negative year-on-year growth five quarters later, in 2024Q4. Through November 2025 the satellite and INE agree to within one log point. A pre-break SARIMA trained through November 2025 projects a 2026 PIB contraction of approximately 2 percent, consistent with the IMF (-3.3 percent), World Bank (-3.2), and IIF (-4) forecasts, though the confidence interval is wide. The centered-12month March 2026 endpoint becomes fully observable from actual data in October 2026, and we commit to a revisit at that date. The indicator is reproducible from free Copernicus data with a two-month publication lag.

title: Rent Effects of Proximity to Gen-AI-Exposed Workplaces in the Post-ChatGPT Era: Evidence from New York City

detail.title: Rent Effects of Proximity to Gen-AI-Exposed Workplaces in the Post-ChatGPT Era: Evidence from New York City

declarations.funderStatement: Thank you for the support from Reading Real Estate Foundation Seed Funding.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how proximity to workplaces in industries highly exposed to Generative AI shapes rent growth in New York City's multifamily built-to-rent (BTR) market following the public release of ChatGPT in November 2022. I construct a composite Generative AI exposure measure for each BTR property by combining SafeGraph geocoded points of interest with Advan foot traffic data, capturing the average Gen-AI exposure of workplaces located within a 30-minute transit travel time based on 2019 baseline commuting patterns. Properties above the citywide median exposure are defined as treated. Employing a difference-indifferences framework, I estimate the differential evolution of rents in BTR properties located near highly exposed employment clusters. The results show a post-ChatGPT decline in rental premiums in these areas, particularly for smaller units such as studios and one-bedrooms. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, I use WageScape job postings to measure changes in both hiring intensity and the skill content of vacancies in nearby labour markets, and I draw on the New York City Housing and Vacancy Survey (NYCHVS) to assess whether exposed housing markets experienced changes in the demographic and socioeconomic composition of resident households. The findings suggest that Gen-AI affects urban rental markets not only through labour demand shocks, but also through occupational restructuring, skill reallocation, and household sorting across neighbourhoods. These results provide evidence on how AI-driven changes in local labour markets transmit into urban rental demand, with implications for institutional investors and policymakers.

title: Evidencing Responsible AI in Financial Services: A Multi-Objective Operations Research Framework, Introducing the MORAI Framework: Pareto Frontiers, Goal Programming, and Stochastic Dominance Testing for Credit Model Compliance

detail.title: Evidencing Responsible AI in Financial Services: A Multi-Objective Operations Research Framework, Introducing the MORAI Framework: Pareto Frontiers, Goal Programming, and Stochastic Dominance Testing for Credit Model Compliance

detail.abstract: The responsible AI (RAI) compliance landscape in financial services is characterised by fragmented disclosure frameworks, inconsistent metric choices, and fundamentally inadequate evidentiary standards. Existing approaches produce binary compliance claims — a model either passes or fails a fairness threshold — that are epistemically brittle, legally vulnerable, and commercially unactionable. This paper argues that the production of responsible AI evidence is, at its core, a multi-objective optimisation (MOO) problem: practitioners must simultaneously balance predictive discrimination, demographic fairness, explanatory fidelity, and operational robustness — objectives that are structurally in tension and cannot be co-maximised without explicit trade-off analysis

title: Risky Insurance: Life-Cycle Insurance Portfolio Choice with Incomplete Markets

detail.title: Risky Insurance: Life-Cycle Insurance Portfolio Choice with Incomplete Markets

publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We study consumer demand for savings, life insurance, annuities, and long-term care insurance using novel survey data and a structural life-cycle model. We document that individuals perceive substantial insurance nonpayment risk, and these beliefs predict ownership. Embedding elicited beliefs into an incomplete-markets model alongside additional real-world insurance features, we match empirical patterns of low participation. Relative to a no-insurance benchmark, access to existing imperfect insurance reduces median wealth by 16% and generates a modest 0.6% welfare gain. Eliminating nonpayment risk would substantially increase insurance ownership, yield a further 11% decline in median savings, and generate an additional 1.7% welfare gain.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: The Safe Side of Shadow Banking
affiliations: University of Sussex Business School, Queen Mary University London, University of Macedonia, Durham Business School and University of Cyprus - Department of Public and Business Administration

detail.title: The Safe Side of Shadow Banking
detail.abstract: We construct lender-specific geopolitical risk indices that vary across shadow and commercial banks. Under geopolitical stress, shadow banks rebalance toward safer borrowers four times more aggressively than commercial banks, committing larger volumes at compressed spreads and concentrating larger capital in higher-quality deals. These deal-level choices aggregate into measurable portfolio-level improvement with compressed risk dispersion. We find that the spread differential between shadow and commercial bank facilities narrows during geopolitical stress, as shadow bank participation compresses equilibrium spreads. Commercial banks tighten the supply of lending, displacing moderate-risk borrowers who represent quality upgrades for shadow banks, qualifying the prediction that lending migration uniformly increases shadow bank risk. A stacked difference-in-differences around ten geopolitical events and Jordà local projections converge on the same persistence pattern.

title: Market Failures Within Algorithmic Pricing: The Information Asymmetry Ethics Behind Surveillance Pricing and Consumer Privacy

detail.title: Market Failures Within Algorithmic Pricing: The Information Asymmetry Ethics Behind Surveillance Pricing and Consumer Privacy
detail.abstract: As companies increasingly favor algorithmic pricing methods to maximize profits, surveillance based information asymmetry is becoming prevalent for consumers among the realms of data privacy. Personalized pricing has various trade-offs, as demonstrated by the model's ability to benefit certain groups (like companies or individuals willing to pay less). However, algorithmic pricing also attains the inability to enforce purchasing parity among all groups of shoppers while creating negative externalities for shoppers due to the seemingly undisclosed nature of the information these models utilize. After studying the frameworks behind how algorithmic pricing models cause market inefficiencies, the most effective ways to improve triadic governance and socio-economical disequilibriums between shoppers, companies, and regulators are nestled in balancing profit optimization with market integrity. This can be achieved through a multidisciplinary approach involving legal systemic transparency methods for surveillance pricing (like petitioning a federal Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act already being implemented within certain states). It can also involve companies branding these bills as a part of their Corporate and Social Responsibilities to incentivize brand loyalty within shoppers, and allow more equitable methods for untapped consumers to enter the market by implementing lower entry barriers. This model and approach reduces negative externalities caused by surveillance pricing, including possible data shielding methods used by consumers which further hurt a company's profits, and allow for untapped consumers to enter new markets without existing consumers being unknowingly impacted, thus further stimulating brand loyalty and eroding market failures in the long run.

title: The Rise of American Esports--and the Fall of the NCAA

detail.title: The Rise of American Esports--and the Fall of the NCAA
detail.abstract: This paper critically examines the financial, structural, and ethical challenges facing collegiate athletics, with a particular focus on esports and Division I programs. It highlights the escalating costs and reliance on institutional subsidies that threaten the sustainability of university sports departments, as well as the shifting landscape caused by NCAA deregulation, NIL (Name, Image, Likeness) policies, and Title IX litigation. The analysis contends that top-tier collegiate athletes are, in effect, professionals and questions the NCAA's use of the “student-athlete” label to justify inequitable treatment. The discussion explores the consequences of pay-for-play models, the inadequacy of scholarships as compensation, and the ongoing struggle for fair wages and rights among athletes. Ultimately, the paper argues for a more just and transparent collegiate sports regime, calling attention to the need for reforms that address both gender equity and the professional status of student-athletes.

title: Free the Agents-Sexism and Misogyny in the Esports Business

detail.title: Free the Agents-Sexism and Misogyny in the Esports Business
detail.abstract: This paper explores the ongoing struggle for gender equity within the esports industry, using recent events as a lens to examine broader societal conflicts over Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) in America. It highlights the challenges faced by women in esports, such as sexism, misogyny, and barriers to representation, illustrated by the activism of players like Josefine Jensen. The analysis connects these experiences to larger trends—intensified resistance to DEI initiatives, legislative and social pushback, and the strategic adaptation of civil rights tactics by opponents of equity. The paper further discusses legal avenues for recourse, such as filing discrimination charges with the EEOC, while acknowledging the limitations of institutional protections amid rising anti-DEI sentiment. Through analogy and contemporary examples, the paper underscores the importance of leveraging economic and cultural influence to advance inclusion, and argues that the evolving dynamics in sports and entertainment may offer new pathways for marginalized groups to contest exclusionary practices and reshape the status quo.

title: Learning for Sustainability in Business Schools: Eco-Consciousness, Curriculum Integration, and Student Readiness for Sustainable Management
affiliations: University of Reading - Henley Business School,, University of Reading - Business Informatics and Systems Accounting Department, University of Bath - School of Management, University of York - The York Management School and University of Reading - ICMA Centre

detail.title: Learning for Sustainability in Business Schools: Eco-Consciousness, Curriculum Integration, and Student Readiness for Sustainable Management

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was received for the survey and the research overall from all three universities involved.

detail.abstract: As global climate challenges intensify, preparing future managers to engage meaningfully with sustainability has become an increasingly central concern for business schools. This study examines how learning about eco-consciousness for sustainability is developed through business school curricula, focusing on business students across three highly ranked universities in England. Drawing on a large and diverse student survey, we investigate both belief-based (personal sustainability values) and experience-based (perceived curriculum integration) drivers that shape students’ learning outcomes in management education, especially their motivation and confidence to incorporate sustainability in future managerial practice. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, we combine Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling with a thematic analysis of open-ended responses. Quantitative findings show that perceived sustainability relevance and curriculum integration significantly enhance students’ motivation and confidence. Valuing sustainability does not directly enhance confidence, but it positively impacts motivation. Qualitative insights deepen these findings by revealing students’ concerns about greenwashing, institutional constraints and dominant logics, perceived powerlessness within corporate contexts, and a strong desire for experiential, embedded, and values-aligned learning opportunities. We propose actionable curricula and pedagogical practices that foster eco-conscious capabilities through reflective, interdisciplinary, and real-world learning. This study contributes theory-informed empirical evidence on the links between cognitive variables in a multi-institutional UK context and advances a conceptual model of student readiness for sustainable management. We conclude by calling for a shift in business education towards the curriculum-wide integration of sustainability, institution-level eco-culture, and greater student agency, and by highlighting the role of learning design in enabling institutional change toward more regenerative forms of management education.

title: Sustainability of AI Infrastructure and Knowledge Management and Monitoring: Investigating the Energy-Water Nexus of Data Center Buildouts in Asia and Pacific Island Countries

detail.title: Sustainability of AI Infrastructure and Knowledge Management and Monitoring: Investigating the Energy-Water Nexus of Data Center Buildouts in Asia and Pacific Island Countries

detail.abstract: The accelerating deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems is generating a surge in data center construction across the Asia-Pacific region, with profound and underexamined sustainability consequences for Pacific Island Countries (PICs). This article investigates the sustainability of AI infrastructure through the integrating lens of Knowledge Management and Monitoring (KMM), arguing that disciplined monitoring architectures are not peripheral administrative tools but the foundational governance instruments determining whether AI infrastructure imposes or alleviates environmental burdens in fragile Pacific host jurisdictions. Drawing on systematic secondary data synthesis, life-cycle assessment (LCA) frameworks, power grid topology analysis, and comparative governance review, this study examines the energy and water demands of representative data center configurations across Pacific jurisdictions including Fiji,

title: Electricity Markets as a Sabzi Mandi: Market Microstructure Lessons from Indian Power Exchanges

detail.title: Electricity Markets as a Sabzi Mandi: Market Microstructure Lessons from Indian Power Exchanges
detail.abstract: This paper examines Indian electricity markets through the analogy of traditional agricultural spot marketslocally known as sabzi mandisto illuminate fundamental dynamics of price discovery, bidding behavior, volatility, and allocation efficiency in formal power exchanges. While electricity markets operate through sophisticated exchange mechanisms such as the Day-Ahead Market (DAM), Real-Time Market (RTM), and Green Day-Ahead Market (GDAM), many of their underlying behavioral and structural dynamics bear a striking resemblance to informal commodity markets characterized by perishable goods, fluctuating supply, demand shocks, strategic bidding, and time-sensitive clearing decisions. Drawing on market microstructure theory, auction design literature, and practitionerinformed perspectives on Indian power markets, this paper develops a four-proposition analytical framework that maps key behavioral driversperishability-induced urgency, information asymmetry, behavioral volatility, and flexibility premiafrom the mandi context onto power exchange outcomes. The study argues that informal market analogies, far from being mere rhetorical devices, offer structurally valid insights into improving efficiency, procurement strategy, and market design in emerging power markets. The paper proceeds in eight sections: following this introduction, Section 2 establishes the sabzi mandi as a rigorous economic analogy rather than a stylistic metaphor. Section 3 maps the structure of Indian power exchanges. Section 4 develops the four core microstructure propositions. Section 5 presents illustrative case examples. Section 6 discusses implications for utility procurement strategy. Section 7 offers policy recommendations. Section 8 concludes with reflections on what formal markets can learn from informal ones.

title: Insulated Leaders: Market Share and Earnings Cyclicality

detail.title: Insulated Leaders: Market Share and Earnings Cyclicality
detail.abstract: High-market-share firms face costs of capital that are more insulated from monetary policy cycles and, in turn, have smoother investment compared to their lower-share competitors. These gaps are robust to the inclusion of financial constraints and size, providing an alternative to standard financial-frictions explanations of monetary transmission. We propose that leaders build inelastic demand that insulates their cash flows from aggregate shocks, and the resulting smoother earnings translate into a more stable cost of capital. Text analysis of earnings call transcripts shows that leaders' disclosures emphasize themes consistent with customer lock-in and franchise value, and the prevalence of such language predicts the cross-sectional pattern in earnings and cost of capital cyclicality. As a consequence, monetary policy transmits more strongly to followers within industries, with persistent implications for industry concentration.

title: Behavioral Responses to Spatial Tax Notches in the Retail Gasoline Market

detail.title: Behavioral Responses to Spatial Tax Notches in the Retail Gasoline Market
detail.abstract: I document long-run spatial distortions at U.S. state borders, where gasoline excise taxes change discretely. Using daily price and location data for the near-universe of U.S. gasoline retailers, I employ a geographic regression discontinuity and two-step fixed-effects analysis. At the border, high-tax-side retailer density is 17 percent lower. The price-tax association there is strictly below one-for-one at 63 to 77 percent, compared to 84 to 89 percent on the low-tax side,  indistinguishable from one-for-one. These gaps close within 15 miles inland. This asymmetry reveals how cross-border competition splits the tax burden between firms and consumers.

title: Operational IP Debt: How AI-Driven Organizations Lose IP Value Before the Law Ever Applies

detail.title: Operational IP Debt: How AI-Driven Organizations Lose IP Value Before the Law Ever Applies
detail.abstract:
Modern technology organizations lose intellectual property value not in courtrooms but in the ordinary operation of their development systems. This Article introduces Operational IP Debt — the progressive loss of forensic reconstructability across an organization’s IP assets, such that assets function commercially but fail when external actors demand proof of ownership, inventorship, provenance, or control. Unlike technical debt, which degrades internal performance on a gradient, Operational IP Debt is externally triggered, latent until stressed, and often irreversible once evidence windows close.

The Article makes three contributions. First, it defines Operational IP Debt as a distinct category of systemic failure, distinguished from technical debt by three structural asymmetries: visibility, continuity, and remediability. It identifies four accumulation vectors — Capture, Evidence, Exposure, and Execution — and shows that every major stress event activates all four simultaneously.

Second, it demonstrates that Operational IP Debt creates adverse selection dynamics (analogous to Akerlof’s market for lemons) in IP transactions: buyers cannot distinguish high-integrity portfolios from degraded ones, producing systematic undervaluation.

Third, it proposes a maturity model that measures forensic reconstructability across four debt vectors and five maturity levels. The model identifies Level 3 as a phase transition: the threshold at which an organization’s evidence infrastructure becomes self-sustaining. It establishes that Evidence maturity is the controlling variable, bounding the legal value of improvements in the other three vectors.

The legal standards are not new. The operational failures are not new. What is new is the framework that explains why organizations that satisfy neither remain unaware of the gap until a stress event converts invisible debt into irreversible asset loss.

title: Covenant Distance and Credit Tightening: Step-Ups, Workouts, and Liquidation Near Default
affiliations: Southern Illinois University - Department of Economics

detail.title: Covenant Distance and Credit Tightening: Step-Ups, Workouts, and Liquidation Near Default
detail.abstract: Bank lending depends on the threat of tougher terms when a borrower misbehaves. This paper shows that the threat has a built-in failure point. As the borrower weakens, she needs harsher threats to be deterred but can absorb only gentler ones. In a model where default is permanent, the two collide at a unique, closed-form cutoff that partitions the state space into discipline, liquidation, and waiver. Below it, every punishment that works also kills the relationship: discipline vanishes at a point, not along a gradient. The cutoff sits in the last third of initial distance to default. It explains why tightening arrives in jumps, why two borrowers with the same breach face different outcomes depending on recovery values, and why sorting breaks down when the lender's signal is noisy. A common shock triples the fraction of loans that lose discipline. The same collision arises wherever punishment can permanently destroy its target.

title: Why Indian Students Must Build AI Literacy Now: Evidence from an Engineering Student Survey

detail.title: Why Indian Students Must Build AI Literacy Now: Evidence from an Engineering Student Survey
detail.abstract: This paper examines the level of AI literacy among Indian engineering students and argues that developing such literacy is urgent for future employability and responsible technology use. Drawing on a survey of 20 students from institutions across Maharashtra, India, conducted between April 22-23, 2026, this study measures awareness of AI concepts, current usage of AI tools, perceived benefits and risks, and self-reported preparedness for an AI-driven job market. The results indicate that while 95% of respondents have heard of generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and Gemini, only 15% report an understanding of AI concepts at a good or expert level, and even fewer feel genuinely confident about using these tools critically or responsibly. Approximately 65% of respondents use AI tools daily or multiple times per day, revealing a sharp disconnect between frequency of use and depth of understanding. Many students express anxiety about future unemployment, confusion about the ethical boundaries of AI use, and a pattern of over-reliance on AI for academic submissions without developing underlying conceptual knowledge. Based on these findings and existing literature on AI literacy

title: Where Does the Marginal Methane Molecule Come From? Implications of LNG Exports for US Natural Gas Supply and Methane Emissions

detail.title: Where Does the Marginal Methane Molecule Come From? Implications of LNG Exports for US Natural Gas Supply and Methane Emissions
detail.abstract: US exports of liquefied natural gas have surged over the past decade and are projected to more than double again by 2030 as more capacity is built. This has raised concerns about upward pressure on domestic energy prices as well as increased methane emissions from expanded oil and gas production. The magnitude of potential increases in natural gas prices depends on the how much US supply is anticipated to respond, and impacts on methane emissions will depend on which oil and gas basins will come from because methane leaks from vary dramatically across basins. Using a dataset on more than 1 million US oil and gas wells, I model the spatially heterogeneous supply responses to US export demand for both US natural gas and crude oil to estimate the impacts on domestic energy prices and the effective methane leak rates of marginal supply. Gas export demand mostly spurs marginal gas supply from Appalachia where methane leak rates are low (1.7% versus 3.1% nationwide average). Oil export demand mostly spurs production from the Permian Basin with high effective leak rates (9.1%). Gas export demand drives larger gas price effects (+2.5% per billion cubic feet/day) than estimated in other studies, while oil export demand has smaller impacts on oil prices (+0.8% per 100k barrels/day).

title: Enforcement and Institutional Change: Union Empowerment and Democratic Labor Relations under the USMCA RRM

detail.title: Enforcement and Institutional Change: Union Empowerment and Democratic Labor Relations under the USMCA RRM

keywords.keywords: Institutional Union Empowerment; Democratic Union Relations; Rapid Response Mechanism; USMCA

detail.abstract: The USMCA Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) is the first tool of its kind to promote the enforcement of labor rights in signatory countries, in this case Mexico. While a growing body of literature and public debates has assessed it after six years in place, there is a lack of studies explaining its impact on labor relations from the perspective of workers involved in cases presented under its umbrella. This paper is based on interviews conducted by LeClercq, Covarrubias and Quintero (2024) and builds upon their main findings in order to address this gap and the question regarding its effectiveness to empower workers and labor unions at the workplace level. Findings confirm statistically significant improvements in collective bargaining performance, collective bargaining legitimization, and labor rights awareness associated with RRM activation. Regression estimates and correlation structures indicate systemic transformation of institutional union power across workplaces, supporting a shift toward democratic labor governance. At this workplaces level, continuous enforcement is needed to maintain these effects and avoid regression into Mexican historical patterns of labor control.

title: Global Adaptive Equity Pricing (GAEP): A Theoretical Model of AI-Enabled Consumption-Based Redistribution

detail.title: Global Adaptive Equity Pricing (GAEP): A Theoretical Model of AI-Enabled Consumption-Based Redistribution
detail.abstract: This paper proposes Global Adaptive Equity Pricing (GAEP), a novel AI-driven framework for moderating economic inequality through real-time, consumption-event-based price personalization. At each domestic purchase, biometric verification links to encrypted networth data to compute a progressive adjusted price using the Wealth Elasticity Pricing Equation (WEPE). Excess payments from higher-net-worth individuals fund a transparent Gini Moderation Fund (GMF) for AI-optimized redistribution targeting a blended Gini coefficient of ≈0.30. Tunable parameters enable governments to control moderation velocity, balancing equity gains against capital retention risks in wealth-attracting jurisdictions. Calibrated to Singapore's 2025-2026 data (income Gini after transfers and taxes: 0.379; market income Gini before transfers: 0.452; wealth Gini: 0.55; top 1% hold ~14%, top 5% ~33% of household wealth), agent-based simulations project 15-41% Gini reductions over 20 quarterly cycles. Ethical safeguards include zero-knowledge proofs, blockchain-audited aggregates (no personal data exposure), fairness audits, and positive incentives. GAEP extends Gini theory and computational economics by integrating biometric technology with redistributive algorithms, distinct from usage-tiered tariffs or surveillance pricing. It offers policymakers a pathway for dynamic, consumption-led equity in AI-augmented economies while preserving innovation incentives.

title: Data Centers, Property Governance, and the Middle-Income Trap: Toward a Concept of Infrastructural Poverty

detail.title: Data Centers, Property Governance, and the Middle-Income Trap: Toward a Concept of Infrastructural Poverty
detail.abstract: As artificial intelligence reshapes the global economy, data centers have become the defining land-intensive infrastructure of the digital age. This paper examines whether cross-national variation in land and property governance helps explain uneven data centerrelated digital infrastructure accumulation. Because data centers require site assembly, property registration, regulatory coordination, and reliable public infrastructure, they are shaped by institutional conditions that vary systematically across countries and income groups. Using a country-year panel of up to 168 countries, merged from UN Comtrade, the World Bank Doing Business historical archive (2010-2020), the World Development Indicators, and the Worldwide Governance Indicators, the paper tests whether property transaction costs, land administration quality, and infrastructure reliability are associated with two distinct layers of digital infrastructure: hardware-related inflows and hostingrelated footprint. Property registration cost is a significant negative predictor of hardware inflows in two-way fixed-effects models. This effect does not extend to hosting footprint, which responds primarily to development level. Interaction and split-sample tests show that the property cost effect is less pronounced in middle-income countries, consistent with a structural positioning interpretation: MICs face higher baseline property friction and exhibit a weaker within-country association between property cost changes and hardware inflows. The findings suggest that, in middle-income contexts, longer-run land-governance capacity-building may matter more than narrowly cost-focused reform for improving digital absorptive conditions.
